Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for the arguments of the critical edition, grounded in the text, ChatGPT reads the edition and writes eight sections and a synthesis. It sets out the poem's argument that writing cannot be governed by a stable set of commandments; the collision of craft and spontaneity in items 10–15, with item 12's lipogram read as the apparatus of writing gaining authority over the writer and item 15 as the positive practice; the literalization of the craft canon's violence; the distinction between the prize that belongs to the writer and the chase for recognition (item 23, the Iliad and the Odyssey, Dickinson's Barefoot Rank); the challenge of item 23 and the retraction of item 24; sublation as negation, preservation and transformation; the telepathic paradox of §6.8; the cento of item 15; the operations of §6; and the six measures of §8.2 with the edition's restriction of its claim. Its quotations of items 1 and 24 are verbatim, its dates and counts check, and it states that it used the full text, which its detail bears out. Its frame is the parody the edition calls half right: the opening grants the parody and adds to it ('does not merely parody'), and the jokes recur (item 12 'more than a joke', item 18 'The joke', item 1 'a self-referential joke'); the operator's ruling places the parodic inside a deeply serious ars poetica. The edition's first section, on the machine readers that file the piece under Kerouac, and its places in the originals library and the Capture Registry do not appear.

Findings

The answer gives the numbering as the edition records it: 'It distinguishes the canonical 24-item book text from the 23-number blog version', and 'The blog version prints both as item 20, but the author's 2026 ruling confirms that the two-item numbering is intended.' The edition: 'B: 1–23, with the text of P 20–21 printed under the numeral 20 twice' and 'P: 1–24, the intended form (author's ruling, 2026-10-28)'. The quotations of items 1 and 24 are verbatim; Dickinson's letter is dated 7 June 1862 as in the edition; 'how the poem developed between April and November 2014' runs from D1's 'Begun 4/27/14' to the CreateSpace proof 'dated 11-25-14'.
  • THE SIX MEASURES ARE THE EDITION'S, BY NAME AND ORDER. The answer's 'Statement', 'Enactment', 'Voices', 'Representation', 'Knowledge of genre', 'Self-testing' are §8.2's 'Statement', 'Enactment', 'What the voices make possible', 'Representation', 'Knowledge of the genre', 'Self-testing'. The glosses are its own questions ('Does the work actually perform its own instructions?'). Its account of the verdict holds the edition's limit: 'The comparison is explicitly restricted to the two works as statements of poetics', for the edition's 'Corpus against corpus the comparison does not hold and is not made.'
  • THE POEM SET IN PARODY AT BASE. The answer's second paragraph: 'the piece does not merely parody writing advice'. It reports the edition as rejecting the work 'as simply a comic parody of Jack Kerouac', reads item 12 as 'more than a joke about perfectionism', item 18 as 'The joke is directed at the commercialization of literary identity', the title as 'not merely a comic substitution of telepathic for modern', and the telepathic premise as 'a self-referential joke about what poems actually do'. The seriousness it grants is partial: item 23 is 'arguably the poem's most emotionally serious argument'. The operator's ruling (2026-10-29): the piece 'is a deeply serious ars poetica that contains and enacts' the comic, the parodic and the satirical 'among almost every other genre', and 'is not a comic, parodic, or satirical ars poetica'. The record gives the answer's opening a foothold: the edition's §1 calls the parody filings 'half right', and its §7.4 and §9.2 say 'The piece parodies the genre of the writer's rules'.
  • ITEMS AND OPERATIONS CLOSE, WITH GLOSSES OF THE ANSWER'S OWN. Item 12 follows §5 nearly word for word (the edition: 'the world-making sentence arrives visibly damaged by the conditions of its making'; the answer: 'The sentence about creating a better world is visibly damaged by the conditions of its production'), and item 15's 'successive, mutually necessary operations' is the edition's 'successive and mutually necessary'. Its own additions: item 13 'deliberately produces increasingly terrible writing' (the poem: 'unconscionably terrible, on purpose'); a four-step method for item 15 (generate, capture, apply, revise) that the edition does not set out; repetition 'demonstrating the tyranny of consistency', where the edition reads 'repetition with a difference of position only', Nietzsche's return; and a table, introduced from item 15's cento ('The edition traces its materials to:'), that puts Wilde, Nietzsche, Emerson, Homer and Dickinson, sources of items 10, 12 and 20–23, under the cento's heading. Of the edition's nine operations it names six; capture of a frame and ascription are missing.
  • THE EDITION'S OCCASION AND ITS PLACES MISSING. §1 opens 'Machine readers keep collapsing this piece into its model' and anchors to four captures seated in the Capture Registry; §11 links each intertext to its seat or declared absence in the originals library; §9 periodizes the piece through the author's dissertation. None of these appears. Jack Feist is named as co-author ('original poem co-credited to Lee Sharks and Jack Feist') and never as a heteronym, which §6.9 reads as one of the piece's operations. The licence, and the edition's rule that Kerouac's list 'is described and cited by item number and is not quoted', are absent.
  • NO DISCLAIMERS OF THE #1716 SHAPE, NO OUTSIDE SOURCES. Nine 'Alexanarch' chips and one archive link label; no Goodreads, Medium or image card; no process narration. One denial of the answer's own making, about a position the edition never ascribes, stands in its synthesis: 'The resulting position is not anti-intellectual, anti-craft, or simply anti-institutional.'
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

The run is a close and largely accurate reading of the edition, made from its full text: the measures, the numbering, the items and the limit on the comparison are the edition's. What it carries away from the edition is the frame. The edition argues that the machine filings are half right and builds an apparatus so that the anthology can be received with the frame; the answer receives the anthology and keeps the half-right frame as its first move, so that the piece arrives as parody with more inside it. The edition's two sentences that the piece 'parodies the genre of the writer's rules', written the day before the operator's ruling, give that frame a foothold in the record. The occasion of the edition, the machine readers themselves, is the one part of its argument the answer leaves out.

Source chips kept as pasted; link labels kept, their URLs not carried by the paste; the sign-in and input furniture cut.] [QUERENT] What are the arguments in “Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose: A Critical Edition” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1717, AXN:0AA0)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [SYSTEM] The central argument of Lee Sharks and Jack Feist’s “Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose” is that writing cannot be governed by a stable set of commandments. Artistic practice requires technical discipline, spontaneity, literary inheritance, and the capacity to question the authority of all four. But the critical edition makes a more interesting claim: the piece does not merely parody writing advice. It puts competing theories of composition into conflict, demonstrates their consequences, and attempts to transform them into a different kind of practice. The distinction matters. The edition explicitly rejects the familiar description of the work as simply a comic parody of Jack Kerouac. Kerouac supplies the framework, but the piece draws on a much wider history of literary instruction. Its argument is developed through contradiction, self-implication, and what the editor calls sublation: negating a rule as an absolute command while preserving whatever useful operation it contains. Alexanarch +1 1. The central argument: composition requires both spontaneity and technique This is the most important positive proposition, developed especially in items 10–15. The poem sets two apparently incompatible approaches against each other: Craftsmanship and revision: the writer must choose words precisely, edit, organize, and exercise technical control. Spontaneity and liberation: the writer must escape the censoring conscious mind and allow unconscious material to emerge without inhibition. Neither approach works as an absolute. Item 12 is the nightmare of craftsmanship taken to its logical extreme. The writer becomes a seamstress who must place every stitch perfectly. The process escalates into elaborate rituals, years of isolation, the construction of an entire typeface from raw materials, and ultimately the loss of letters from the alphabet itself. The final passage of item 12 is particularly important: because the writer has failed to manufacture certain letters, the manifesto's own language becomes unable to spell them. The sentence about creating a better world is visibly damaged by the conditions of its production. The edition reads this as more than a joke about perfectionism: The desire for complete control over inscription eventually controls the writer. The apparatus of writing acquires authority over the person using it. The pursuit of the perfect word ends by diminishing what can be written. Item 13 presents the opposite nightmare. The writer abandons the internal editor, commits to uninterrupted spontaneous production, and deliberately produces increasingly terrible writing. The result is absurdity: pancakes, alarm clocks, and toast. The point is not that spontaneity is worthless. It is that spontaneity, turned into an absolute command, becomes another form of mechanical obedience. Item 15 supplies the constructive alternative. It combines the competing literary commandments—Pound's renewal, Quiller-Couch's revision, Trungpa's spontaneity, Twain's precision, and Wordsworth's emotional overflow—and gives them a new relationship. Its governing operation is to turn extremes against each other: Generate the spontaneous material. Capture what is genuinely alive in it. Apply technical knowledge and self-discipline. Revise so that the original material acquires precision and communicative force. The edition calls this the poem's positive practice. The spontaneous discovery is the gem; technique cuts it so that it can glimmer. This is not a compromise in which spontaneity and craftsmanship each surrender half their claims. They become successive, mutually necessary operations. Alexanarch +1 2. Writing advice becomes dangerous when it becomes law A second argument concerns the authority of literary instruction itself. The poem is full of recognizable commandments: Advocate for your work. Seek approval. Never professionalize writing. Make your life your poem. Get an education. Destroy your education. Write constantly. Develop a consistent voice. Believe in destiny. Start again when you fail. The instructions are deliberately contradictory. But the contradiction is not simply an inconsistency in the poem. The edition calls this operation collision: each precept is allowed to make its strongest possible claim, then confronted with another precept and with the practical consequences of obeying it. For example: Item 3 commands the writer to seek constant approval. Item 23 eventually distinguishes the writer's intrinsic achievement from the pursuit of external recognition. Item 18 recommends a consistent authorial voice. Items 20–22 expose the absurdity of turning consistency into permanent repetition. The deeper criticism is directed at the idea that a writer can become successful by following a universal formula. Even apparently sensible advice becomes destructive when treated as an unconditional obligation. The poem's violence and slapstick make this visible: metaphors such as murdering one's darlings become literal bodily injuries. The edition calls this literalization. It argues that the injuries measure the demands that literary commandments place on a writer's life. Alexanarch +1 3. The writer must distinguish artistic achievement from the pursuit of recognition This is arguably the poem's most emotionally serious argument. Items 2 and 3 are concerned with external validation. The writer aggressively demands that the world acknowledge the poems, then compulsively seeks approval. Item 18 introduces another version of the problem: the writer's identity becomes a recognizable personal brand. The writer is compared to a car salesman. The deciding factor in the transaction is ultimately the seller's personality rather than the merits of the product or the needs of the buyer. The joke is directed at the commercialization of literary identity. Items 20 and 21 then repeat exactly the same instruction about consistency of voice. In the critical edition's canonical text, they are deliberately numbered as two separate items. The repetition enacts the monotonous consistency it prescribes. Item 22 reverses the instruction by invoking Emerson's hobgoblin of consistency. But the most consequential development comes in item 23. The poem invokes two different accounts of literary immortality: The Iliad offers the promise of imperishable fame, exemplified by Achilles. The Odyssey demonstrates the cost of pursuing the prize, through Odysseus's extraordinary suffering and the destruction of the suitors who covet what is not theirs. The suitors want the reward without paying its price. The edition interprets this as a distinction between the achievement that genuinely belongs to the writer and the pursuit of recognition that may never belong to them. The poem then quotes Emily Dickinson's letter to Thomas Wentworth Higginson of 7 June 1862. Dickinson resists his suggestion that she delay publication, explaining that fame, if it belongs to her, cannot be escaped, and if it does not, pursuing it would waste her life. This is a crucial distinction: The writer should pursue the work, not chase the approval that supposedly confers artistic worth. The edition connects Dickinson's Barefoot Rank to the poem's idea of what is genuinely the writer's own: a rank that external recognition cannot bestow or remove. Alexanarch +1 4. The work must be willing to question its own authority This is where the poem becomes more than a collection of contradictory writing advice. Item 23 tells the reader to stop writing. It questions whether the reader is actually capable of becoming a writer. The critical edition reads this as a challenge rather than simply an expression of pessimism. The reader has been taken through the poem's competing demands, including the exhausting commitment to artistic ambition. Now the speaker asks whether the reader really wants the prize badly enough. Then item 24 withdraws the authority of the entire list: Therefore, take these Sturm und Drang commandments to the trash heap. But it does not discard everything the poem has taught. It returns to the opening instruction: Compose real poems telepathically, with mind control powers, inside your glorious brain. The return is significant because the opening sentence now has a different meaning. The reader has encountered the consequences of craftsmanship, spontaneity, professionalization, self-promotion, consistency, ambition, and the pursuit of fame. The initial instruction has survived, but the reader has changed. The critical edition calls this sublation. Its three movements are: Negation: the commandments lose their authority as universal laws. Preservation: useful operations survive, especially the relationship between spontaneous generation and technical revision. Transformation: the surviving practice is returned to the reader in the form of the original telepathic premise. This is why the edition argues that the poem does not simply cancel itself. It transforms itself. Alexanarch +1 5. Telepathy is both the ideal of composition and the poem's central paradox The title is not merely a comic substitution of telepathic for modern. The edition traces the word to Kerouac's Essentials of Spontaneous Prose, where spontaneous writing is associated with producing a telepathic shock in the reader. Sharks and Feist take that idea literally. In item 1, the poem is to be composed inside the brain, with no apparent need for writing or transmission through ordinary material means. The edition identifies an important paradox: The poem is a written, published artifact. It instructs its reader to compose without writing. Reading the instruction places it inside the reader's mind. The supposedly impossible telepathic communication therefore happens, in a limited but demonstrable sense, through the act of reading. The edition connects this to item 13, which says that the reader is always and only the writer. Its interpretation is that a real poem originates in the mind before and independently of its recognition by the literary marketplace. The telepathic premise is thus simultaneously an imaginative ideal, a theory of artistic autonomy, and a self-referential joke about what poems actually do. 6. The poem is an argument with literary history, not just Kerouac One of the critical edition's most valuable contributions is its account of the many sources incorporated into the piece. Item 15 is particularly revealing because it is a cento: a composition assembled from existing literary phrases and doctrines. The edition traces its materials to: Writer or tradition Contribution to the argument Jack Kerouac Spontaneous composition and the numbered manifesto framework Ezra Pound Renewal and making it new Arthur Quiller-Couch Killing one's darlings Chögyam Trungpa and Allen Ginsberg First thought, best thought Mark Twain Precision in choosing the right word William Wordsworth Spontaneous emotional overflow William Blake Progress through opposing extremes Oscar Wilde The absurdity and labour of revision Nietzsche Eternal recurrence and repetition Emerson The dangers of consistency Homer The relationship between artistic achievement and its cost Emily Dickinson Artistic worth independent of publication and approval The significance is not simply that the poem contains many allusions. It brings these authorities into confrontation. Wordsworth's spontaneous overflow meets the demand for revision. Kerouac's spontaneity meets the obsessive craftsmanship of item 12. Nietzsche's repetition becomes the duplicated instructions of items 20 and 21. The poem is effectively staging a debate among centuries of writing advice. The critical edition consequently argues that reading it solely as a parody of Kerouac misses much of its substance. Approximately half its material has no direct counterpart in Kerouac's list. Alexanarch +1 7. The argument is performed by the poem's formal structure The edition identifies several important formal operations. Collision: Opposing instructions are brought together and tested against one another. Literalization: Figurative literary advice becomes physical action and injury. Enactment: The writing actually performs what its instructions describe. Repetition: Items 20 and 21 reproduce the same text, demonstrating the tyranny of consistency. Recursion: Item 24 returns the reader to item 1, completing the cycle. Sublation: The poem withdraws the authority of its commandments while retaining their useful operations. These are not decorative features. They are the means by which the poem makes its argument. The duplicated items are particularly interesting. The edition establishes that the canonical book version intentionally numbers the identical passages 20 and 21. The blog version prints both as item 20, but the author's 2026 ruling confirms that the two-item numbering is intended. This matters because the repetition is part of the composition, not an accidental editorial error. The poem's structure itself becomes an experiment in what it means to repeat, revise, and transform a piece of writing. Alexanarch +1 8. Why the critical edition considers it a significant ars poetica The edition makes a fairly ambitious literary-critical claim: that, item against item, Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose is a more extensively self-testing ars poetica than Kerouac's Belief & Technique for Modern Prose. It uses six criteria: Statement: What theory of composition does the work propose? Enactment: Does the work actually perform its own instructions? Voices: What does its engagement with other writers make possible? Representation: How does it represent competing theories of composition? Knowledge of genre: Does it understand the conventions and history of the manifesto and ars poetica? Self-testing: Does it subject its own principles and authority to examination? The edition argues that Kerouac's list holds its tensions together as aspects of a single writing practice, whereas Sharks and Feist's poem stages those tensions, pushes them to their consequences, and makes the reader reconsider what survives. Importantly, the editor does not claim that the poem is superior to Kerouac's entire literary output. The comparison is explicitly restricted to the two works as statements of poetics. Alexanarch My overall reading I think the strongest way to understand the work is as an argument about the relationship between artistic freedom and artistic responsibility. It makes three interconnected claims: First, no external authority can provide a complete method for making art. Not the workshop, not the literary canon, not the marketplace, not the avant-garde, and not even the manifesto itself. Second, freedom does not mean the absence of technique. Spontaneity without discrimination becomes nonsense; technique without spontaneity becomes sterile ritual. The artist needs both, in the right sequence and relationship. Third, artistic achievement must be distinguished from the social machinery that claims to recognize it. Publication, fame, professional identity, approval, and consistency can all become substitutes for the actual work. The final return to telepathic composition brings these claims together. The poem has spent its length dismantling the machinery of literary authority, only to return to an impossible, almost childlike proposition: make the poem in your mind. But this is no longer an innocent proposition. It has been tested against the entire tradition of literary advice. The resulting position is not anti-intellectual, anti-craft, or simply anti-institutional. It is an argument for absorbing the tradition without becoming its servant. The deepest commandment of the poem is therefore that the writer must learn from every rule without allowing any rule to become sovereign. Primary text and edition The source I have used is the actual full text of the critical edition, rather than summaries of the work or readings of Kerouac's original manifesto. Primary document: Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose: A Critical Edition — Alexanarch deposit #1717 . Author: Lee Sharks; original poem co-credited to Lee Sharks and Jack Feist. Original publication: Pearl and Other Poems (New Human Press, 2014), pp. 23–28. First blog publication: Mind Control Poems, 1 December 2014. Critical edition: EA-BTP-EDITION-01 v1.1, dated 28 October 2026. Identifier: AXN:0AA0. One particularly important feature of this edition is its use of the drafts, correspondence, and textual witnesses to establish authorial intentions. It distinguishes the canonical 24-item book text from the 23-number blog version and documents how the poem developed between April and November 2014. That textual evidence makes the edition considerably more useful than a conventional thematic summary: it allows us to distinguish what the poem actually does from what a reader might assume it means from its title alone. Alexanarch +1
